activities.anchor: Your essay grade depends on saying precisely
activities.caption: bet before you read on — where the machine ran
activities.name: lonThesisPredict

config.q: The thesis to test: the League was a working machine that the great powers stopped operating. Where did the machine actually run?
choices: Nowhere — the design was broken from January 1920
By and for small states that wanted disputes resolved — and nowhere a determined great power stood in the way
Only in Europe, and only before Germany joined in 1926
config.why: Machinery that succeeded in 1921 and 1925 failed in 1931 and 1935 — the design did not change, the will did. Where running it would cost a great power something real, it broke.

activities.caption: pair each organ with its job
activities.name: lonOrganMatch

config.prompt: The Covenant's machine — pair each part with its role:

pairs.right: the great powers' chamber — permanent seats for Britain, France, Italy and Japan; Germany added 1926, the USSR 1934
every member, with one vote each
the paperwork of a world foreign ministry

config.why: Article 16's promise — a collective trade embargo, then the members' combined armies — rested on unanimity for every decision and soldiers no one had to lend: slow, collective and optional.

activities.anchor: The deeper gap was authority no one had surrendered
activities.caption: draft the Covenant yourself, 1919
activities.name: lonDraftingBranch

config.root: Geneva, 1919. You speak for a small state drafting the Covenant. How do you protect yourself?

start.text: The rules of force are yours to write.

choices.label: Insist on unanimity for every decision
choices.feedback: No one can conscript you into a great power's war — and nothing can be decided quickly.

choices.label: Promise troops in advance against any aggressor
choices.feedback: You have volunteered to fight someone else's war, for disputes you never voted on.

choices.label: Give the League a standing army of its own
choices.feedback: No member hands over soldiers in 1919 — the idea dies in committee.

unanimity.text: Written into the Covenant: every decision of Council and Assembly needs unanimous agreement — slow, collective and optional, exactly the combination an aggressor could exploit.

troops.text: No other small state follows you: no member was willing to promise troops for disputes it had not voted on. The idea is dropped.

army.text: There is no League army in the final draft — 'force' means members volunteering to fight someone else's war.

config.why: The design was not stupidity — it was the maximum sovereignty the members would surrender in 1919, which was less than collective security actually required.

activities.anchor: The 1920s record needs judging case by case
activities.caption: line up the cases, earliest first
activities.name: lonCasesOrder

config.prompt: The decade's test cases — order them by date, earliest first:
items: Vilna: Poland seizes the Lithuanian capital and ignores the protest — 1920
Aaland Islands: awarded to Finland, demilitarised, and both accept — 1921
Upper Silesia: a 60–40 plebiscite, then a partition both sides accept — 1921
Corfu: Mussolini bombards; the dispute is settled around the League — 1923
Geneva Protocol: compulsory arbitration, killed by Britain — 1924
config.why: The League could resolve almost any dispute between states that wanted resolving, and none involving a great power willing to use force — a real achievement and a fatal limitation at once.

activities.anchor: The humanitarian and technical record is easier to defend still
activities.caption: file each quiet achievement
activities.name: lonHumanBuckets

config.prompt: The record examiners reward because it is often forgotten — file each piece:

items.label: hundreds of thousands of prisoners of war returned after 1918
the Nansen passport — papers for stateless refugees (Nobel Peace Prize, 1922)
campaigns against typhus, malaria and leprosy — the seed of today's WHO
administering the Saar and Danzig directly
running the referendums that sorted contested borders

config.why: This work saved lives in every decade the League existed — the strongest evidence that 'failure' is too blunt a verdict.

activities.anchor: The Wall Street Crash of October 1929
activities.caption: call the collapse — world trade's value
activities.name: lonCrashEstimate

config.prompt: Between 1929 and 1932, world trade lost roughly what share of its value?
config.why: Roughly two-thirds — tariffs and economic nationalism everywhere, the 1931 banking crises (Austria's Credit-Anstalt, then Germany and Britain off the gold standard), and the Dawes-loan system dead with American credit.
config.context: The Depression made aggressors too: Japan's militarists argued a resource-poor Japan must grab an empire or starve; Mussolini sought cheap imperial glory to distract from economic pain.

activities.anchor: The two great failures teach the same lesson from two directions
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the 1930s record
activities.name: lonFailSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary is wrong — click it:
lines: Manchuria, 1931: officers stage an 'incident' on the South Manchuria railway; the province is renamed Manchukuo under the puppet emperor Puyi.
The Lytton Report takes over a year; the Assembly condemns Japan in February 1933.
Japan resigns in March 1933 — and the League's sanctions bite.
Abyssinia, October 1935: Italy declared the aggressor; half-sanctions follow — no oil embargo.
Britain keeps the Suez Canal open to Italian supply ships throughout; Addis Ababa falls in May 1936.
config.correction: No sanctions were ever even proposed against Japan — Britain's navy was in home waters and no one wanted to fight Japan in Manchuria.
config.why: By 1935 every instrument existed: the Covenant declared Italy the aggressor and sanctions followed within weeks. What failed was enforcement — enough sanction to anger Mussolini, not enough to stop him.

activities.caption: drag the divider — the draft and its rewrite
activities.name: lonAfterlifeCompare

config.prompt: The first draft and its successor — drag the divider:

before.label: The League, 1920
before.text: Unanimity among all members, no army of its own, its own architect standing outside — collective security slow, collective and optional.

after.label: The United Nations, 1945
after.text: Nearly the whole design kept; unanimity replaced by a Security Council of five permanent members with vetoes — concentrating, not escaping, the great-power question.

config.why: Historians now see the League as the necessary first draft: its documented failures — unanimity, no army, no America — became the design requirements of everything attempted since.
